title: Less to lose
hookLine: Diogenes' slave ran away, and Diogenes let him go; fewer things, fewer wounds (On Tranquility 8)

lines: THE WHITE SOFA NO ONE CAN SIT ON.
cards: Have you ever bought something nice and then spent a week worrying about it? The new phone you're scared to drop. The car you check from the window.
The white sofa no one is allowed to eat on. It was meant to make life easier, and it came with a small, permanent alarm attached.
In chapter eight of On Tranquility, Seneca says that of all the things that trouble the mind, the biggest is money and what it buys.
And he tells a story about the philosopher Diogenes, who, tradition says, lived in a large clay jar, on the day his only servant ran away.

teach.h: IT HURTS LESS NOT TO HAVE THAN TO LOSE.
teach.b: First, Seneca's claim. People with little, he says, often suffer less than people with much, not because poverty is pleasant, but because they have less that can be taken.
It hurts less never to have had something than to lose it. Fortune has fewer places to strike. Second, the story.
Diogenes owned one slave, named Manes. Manes ran away. Someone told Diogenes where he'd gone, and Diogenes didn't think it worth the trouble to bring him back.

teach.h: MANES RAN; DIOGENES LET HIM GO.
teach.b: It would be shameful, he said, if Manes could live without Diogenes, and Diogenes couldn't live without Manes.
Third, the honest flinch. The story treats a human being as a possession, as Seneca's whole world did, and it's fair to flinch at that.
But inside it there's something Diogenes may not have meant: Manes walked free, and Diogenes let him. Fourth, the point.

Seneca imagines Diogenes saying to Fortune: mind your own business, there's nothing of yours left here. Fewer things, fewer wounds. Seneca, who owned a great deal, isn't telling anyone to own nothing.
He's asking which of your things own you: the phone you're afraid to drop, the status you'd hate to lose. Each one is a place where a bad day can reach in. Having less isn't the goal by itself.

how: People practicing Stoic simplicity sometimes give away possessions that cause more worry than use, aiming to be harder to wound rather than simply to own less.

o: the Roman goddess of wisdom and good advice
a large sum of money saved up for later
fortune, chance, which can only take what you have

games.q: less to lose — tap the pairs.
p: losing hurts more than not having

s: Diogenes chased his runaway servant to get him back
he thought it shameful to need Manes more than Manes needed him.
Seneca says the biggest trouble for the mind is money and what it buys
it gives Fortune more places to strike.
Seneca tells everyone to own nothing at all
he asks which of your things own you.

games.q: you're Diogenes. your only servant has run off, and someone tells you where he is. what do you do?
games.why: Diogenes let him go: it'd be shameful if Manes could live without Diogenes, but not Diogenes without Manes.

practice: Picture your home and find one thing you worry about more than you enjoy, the one that sets off a small alarm. Imagine it gone, given away or simply not there, and notice what happens in your chest: relief, panic, or both.
Either way, now you know where the alarm is wired.

wordCard.voice: Fortuna. Latin for fortune, chance, which Seneca imagines Diogenes telling to mind its own business: fewer things, fewer places to wound. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, 'Fortune, chance': which Seneca imagines Diogenes telling to mind its own business.

carryVoice: Your line: mind your own business. A lighter house gives fortune less to grab. Day four hundred ninety-nine, done.
